summary.text: Taking \(n=140\), direct floor evaluations (obtained by squaring the relevant rational bounds on \(\sqrt{5/4}\)) give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the proposed right-hand side is \(528+484-471=541\), not \(a(161)=542\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating it at \(n=140\).

First, we compute the four required values \(a(140),a(144),a(157),a(161)\). All square-root floor computations below are exact. We use the elementary fact that, for a nonnegative real number \(X\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\),
\[
k^2\le X<(k+1)^2
\]
implies
\[
k\le \sqrt X<k+1,
\]
and hence \(\lfloor\sqrt X\rfloor=k\). Also, because \(n\ge0\),
\[
n\sqrt{\frac54}=\sqrt{n^2\frac54}.
\]

For \(n=140\), the radicand is
\[
140^2\frac54=19600\cdot\frac54=24500.
\]
Now
\[
156^2=24336\le24500<24649=157^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
156\le140\sqrt{\frac54}<157,
\qquad
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Since \(140/4=35\), we obtain
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(n=144\),
\[
144^2\frac54=20736\cdot\frac54=25920.
\]
The consecutive squares around this number are
\[
160^2=25600\le25920<25921=161^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Also \(144/4=36\), so
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(n=157\),
\[
157^2\frac54=24649\cdot\frac54=\frac{123245}{4}.
\]
We compare this with \(175^2\) and \(176^2\). Written with denominator \(4\), these are
\[
175^2=30625=\frac{122500}{4},
\qquad
176^2=30976=\frac{123904}{4}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
175^2=\frac{122500}{4}
\le \frac{123245}{4}
<\frac{123904}{4}=176^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), and hence
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{157}{4}\right\rfloor=39.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(n=161\),
\[
161^2\frac54=25921\cdot\frac54=\frac{129605}{4}.
\]
Here
\[
180^2=32400=\frac{129600}{4},
\qquad
181^2=32761=\frac{131044}{4}.
\]
Thus
\[
180^2=\frac{129600}{4}
\le\frac{129605}{4}
<\frac{131044}{4}=181^2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
Since \(161=4\cdot40+1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{161}{4}\right\rfloor=40.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

We now test the conjectured recurrence at \(n=140\), which is an allowed index because \(140\ge1\). At this index it asserts
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
The left-hand side is
\[
a(161)=542,
\]
whereas the right-hand side is
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)
=528+484-471
=1012-471
=541.
\]
Thus the asserted equality would be \(542=541\), which is false.

Equivalently, in the order-\(21\) coefficient formulation, the only nonzero coefficients are \(-1\) at offset \(0\), \(1\) at offset \(4\), and \(1\) at offset \(17\); all other offsets contribute zero. Hence the recurrence sum at base index \(140\) reduces precisely to
\[
-a(140)+a(144)+a(157)=541,
\]
while the term at offset \(21\) is \(a(161)=542\). (If the sequence is shifted to \(u(m)=a(m+1)\), this same instance is obtained by taking \(m=139\): then \(u(139+21)=a(161)\) and \(u(139+i)=a(140+i)\).)

Therefore the proposed recurrence does not hold for every \(n\ge1\), and the conjecture is false.
